extracted.intended_audience: experimental scientists, observational astronomers, and students of scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules and theoretical principles for making accurate physical observations: using means and mechanical arrangements to eliminate disturbances, determining zero points and maxima, and treating residual discrepancies by a law of error (least squares/Gaussian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of means to cancel symmetric opposing effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever several causes act so that each at one time increases and at another time decreases the joint effect by equal quantities, apply the method of taking means (e.g. Brahe's pole-star method: half the sum of elevations at upper and lower meridian passages gives the latitude, 'free from doubt, except as regards incidental errors').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pole-star high/low passages; spring = lunar+solar tide, neap = lunar − solar tide (half the sum/difference gives lunar/solar tide). Requires identification of the periods at which a cause acts positively or negatively (a priori knowledge). When applicable, take the mean of observations when the cause acts positively and when it acts negatively; half the difference of these means yields the effect of that cause, provided no other effect varies in the same period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain long series over complete cycles to detect very small effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Small effects can be detected amidst much larger fluctuations only if one has a sufficiently numerous and long continued series of observations covering at least one complete cycle in which the effects run through all their variations and return to the same relative positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If casual/irregular disturbances exist, many cycles may be required to render their effect inappreciable. Example: detection of atmospheric tides at St. Helena by averaging readings when the moon was on the meridian versus on the horizon; differences detected were extremely small (e.g. 0.006 inches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mechanical arrangements to eliminate high-frequency fluctuations
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate, employ physical filtering so only the general/mean change is perceived rather than transient oscillations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: place thermometer bulb a few feet below surface to remove daily variations; at 20 feet reduce yearly fluctuations; tide-gauge float in a cistern communicating by a small hole to exclude surface-wave oscillations; narrow tube in marine barometer to suppress casual fluctuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful determination of the zero point (reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many observations depend chiefly on defining exactly the zero point (e.g. true horizon) from which measurements are made; the choice of method for determining that zero is critical to precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: astronomers generally use the surface of mercury in repose as the criterion of horizontality, observing a star and its reflection and taking the mean between apparent and reflected place as the horizontal (zero) point. Plumb-line is often hopelessly inaccurate because of attraction by nearby masses; choose the most accurate practical criterion for the situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average terminal points of oscillation to find equilibrium/zero for balances
rubrics_metrics.description: When a beam never comes to rest cleanly (friction, impediments), determine the terminal points of its vibrations and use their means to estimate the true rest point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the beam vibrate and observe terminal points; the mean between symmetric terminal points approximates the rest. Take multiple excursions and use formulas (e.g. mean of (a+2b+c)/4 from four readings or J(a+2b+c) from three) and correct for damping (friction, air resistance) by additional observations. Example: Baily's torsion-balance experiments to determine earth's density relied on observing oscillation extremes with and without attracting mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using an absolute zero by differential (reversed) arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Design experiments so uniform disturbances cancel out, eliminating need to know an absolute zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: K. J. Stone's double thermo-electric pile with reversed parts — disturbances acting uniformly on both piles produce no galvanometer effect, while alternating star rays on piles yield twice the star heating effect. Differential/reversal arrangements can reveal minute signals otherwise masked by uniform background effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine maxima by locating equal ordinates on either side and averaging (symmetry-based maxima determination)
rubrics_metrics.description: A variable quantity reaching a maximum usually increases and then decreases by insensible degrees; the maximum is often best located by finding points on either side with equal ordinates and taking their mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure corresponding pairs of points on both sides of the peak and average them; take several such pairs and average the whole set for improved accuracy. This method depends on symmetry of the curve and fails when the law of variation is asymmetric or governed by other rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of applying mean-based methods when the rising and falling laws differ (asymmetry caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures that take simple means to locate events (e.g. times of high water) can fail if the phenomenon follows different laws in rising and falling, or otherwise lacks symmetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Whewell's proposal to take mean of times when water passes a fixed point above/below maximum does not give correct high-water time if tide rises and falls according to different laws. Laplace's reasoning about highest spring tide assumes approximate symmetry; check assumptions of symmetry before applying mean-based shortcuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Average paired observations to remove observer judgment bias
rubrics_metrics.description: When an event's exact moment is indefinite and observer judgment is involved (e.g. eclipses, immersion/emersion), take paired observations under equivalent conditions and average to cancel subjective bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For Jupiter's satellite eclipses, note immersion and emersion times with the same telescope and consistent observer action; the mean of the two times represents the satellite's middle-of-shadow time as increase/decrease laws are reversed and observer bias cancels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat residual unknown discrepancies by a general law of error only after exhausting special corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: If, after accounting for known instrument- or procedure-specific sources of error, residual discrepancies remain of unknown origin, apply a uniform general law of error to handle them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that each instrument/process may have its own special law of error and those should be discovered if possible. The general Law of Error is the best guide only when special sources have been investigated and excluded; it provides a uniform rule for residual, unknown causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt principles for selecting a law of error: rarer large errors and symmetry of sign
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a law of error consistent with (1) large errors being far less frequent than small ones, and (2) positive and negative errors being equally probable, implying the probability is a function of an even power of magnitude (preferably square).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gauss prefers the square (leading to Gaussian) because it satisfies the above and yields tractable formulae; higher even powers would satisfy symmetry but complicate calculations. The choice balances theoretical plausibility and practical simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the least-squares principle to select the most probable estimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Among discrepant results the most probable estimate is the quantity that makes the sum of the squares of the errors as small as possible (method of least squares).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If observations are a,b,c,... and x is the chosen estimate, choose x to minimize (a−x)^2+(b−x)^2+(c−x)^2+... . Historical note: Gauss (d. 1795) advocated this on probabilistic grounds; Legendre published the method in 1806. The rule follows from the Gaussian law of error and is the practical criterion for combining observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate special/specific error-laws when practicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever practicable and worth the labour, investigate distinct causes of error for an instrument or process and determine their specific probability-curves (special laws of error) rather than blindly applying the general law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special laws may be deduced a priori from the nature of causes or a posteriori by observation; examples include studies of particular instruments (e.g. the repeating circle). Bi*avais and others investigated instrument-specific error distributions; do so when those errors are significant and identifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: When many small independent causes combine, expect Gaussian behavior (combinatorial justification)
rubrics_metrics.description: If observation errors arise from a large number of independent, infinitesimal causes, the resultant distribution of errors will tend to the Gaussian form; combinatorial arguments (arithmetical triangle/binomial) show small errors are far more probable than large ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative combinatorial examples: with four independent ±1-inch chances the distribution of total errors follows binomial coefficients; increasing the number of causes while reducing their magnitude yields a law approximating the Gaussian. Reasons for adopting the infinite-many-causes hypothesis: (1) there may be infinitely numerous causes in practice; (2) finite-cause laws approximate the infinite case closely; (3) the infinite hypothesis yields a convenient general law amenable to uniform calculation.
